Reproducible simulation studies

Source: vignettes/articles/simulations.Rmd
simulations.Rmd
library(zurand)

A simulation study runs the same experiment many times, under several scenarios, and compares the results. This article shows how zurand keeps such a study reproducible while it grows, while it runs in parallel and while it is stopped and restarted.

The problem with one global seed

With R’s own generator, every number depends on how many were drawn before it. Here an analysis draws ten values, and then someone adds a single extra draw at the start:

set.seed(1)
before <- rnorm(10)

set.seed(1)
extra <- runif(1)          # one new draw, early in the script
after <- rnorm(10)

identical(before, after)
#> [1] FALSE

Every later result has changed. With zurand, each piece of work draws from its own key, so adding work elsewhere cannot disturb it:

study <- rng_key(2026)
before <- rng_normal(rng_fold(study, "analysis"), 10)

extra <- rng_uniform(rng_fold(study, "new step"), 1)
after <- rng_normal(rng_fold(study, "analysis"), 10)

identical(before, after)
#> [1] TRUE

A key for every part of the study

A study has a natural shape: scenarios, and replicates within each. Fold the study key by the scenario’s name, then by the number of the replicate, and every replicate of every scenario has its own stream:

replicate_key <- function(scenario, r) {
  rng_fold(rng_fold(study, scenario), r)
}

one_run <- function(scenario, r, n = 30) {
  key <- replicate_key(scenario, r)
  shift <- c(null = 0, small = 0.3, large = 0.8)[[scenario]]
  x <- rng_normal(key, n, mean = shift)
  t.test(x)$p.value < 0.05
}

power <- function(scenario, reps = 200) {
  mean(vapply(seq_len(reps), function(r) one_run(scenario, r), logical(1)))
}

results <- c(null = power("null"), small = power("small"))
results
#>  null small 
#> 0.025 0.360

Adding a scenario later leaves the earlier ones exactly as they were, because no scenario’s numbers depend on another’s:

results2 <- c(null = power("null"), small = power("small"),
              large = power("large"))
identical(results, results2[c("null", "small")])
#> [1] TRUE
results2
#>  null small large 
#> 0.025 0.360 0.990

The same holds for more replicates: replicates 1 to 200 are the same whether the study runs 200 or 1,000 of them.

Running in parallel

Because the numbers of each replicate come from its own key, it does not matter which worker runs it, or in which order. No worker needs a seed:

cores <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") 1L else 2L
serial <- vapply(1:100, function(r) one_run("small", r), logical(1))
parallel <- unlist(parallel::mclapply(
  1:100, function(r) one_run("small", r), mc.cores = cores
))
identical(serial, parallel)
#> [1] TRUE

future.apply::future_lapply() or any other parallel map gives the same result. zurand’s own threads work the same way: rng_threads() changes how fast a large draw is made, never its values.

Common random numbers

To compare two methods fairly, give them the same random inputs. The difference between them then reflects the methods, not the luck of the draw. With keys this is just a matter of using the same key for both.

Here two estimators of a centre, the mean and the median, are compared on data with an occasional outlier:

make_data <- function(key, n = 25) {
  x <- rng_normal(key, n)
  outlier <- rng_uniform(rng_fold(key, "outlier"), n) < 0.1
  x + outlier * 8
}

compare <- function(r, shared) {
  k1 <- replicate_key("estimators", r)
  k2 <- if (shared) k1 else rng_fold(k1, "second")
  abs(mean(make_data(k1))) - abs(median(make_data(k2)))
}

diff_shared <- vapply(1:300, compare, numeric(1), shared = TRUE)
diff_indep <- vapply(1:300, compare, numeric(1), shared = FALSE)

rbind(
  shared = c(mean = mean(diff_shared), sd = sd(diff_shared)),
  independent = c(mean = mean(diff_indep), sd = sd(diff_indep))
)
#>                  mean        sd
#> shared      0.5335896 0.4433732
#> independent 0.5308661 0.5043226

Both designs estimate the same average difference, the extra error of the mean from the outliers, but with shared keys the difference in each replicate is less noisy (a smaller sd), so the same precision needs fewer replicates.

Stopping and resuming

A long simulation can draw its random numbers in pieces with offset. Position k of a key’s stream is the same however it is reached, so drawing in batches gives exactly what one long draw would:

key <- rng_fold(study, "long run")
all_at_once <- rng_normal(key, 1000)

batches <- lapply(0:3, function(b) rng_normal(key, 250, offset = 250 * b))
identical(all_at_once, unlist(batches))
#> [1] TRUE

To resume after a stop, all a checkpoint needs to record is how far the run got; the random numbers for the rest follow from the key:

done <- 600                                     # saved at the checkpoint
rest <- rng_normal(key, 1000 - done, offset = done)
identical(rest, all_at_once[(done + 1):1000])
#> [1] TRUE

Saving keys

A key is a small R object. Save it with the results, and anyone can regenerate the exact random numbers later, on any machine:

f <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(study, f)
identical(rng_normal(readRDS(f), 3), rng_normal(study, 3))
#> [1] TRUE
